name: Boson Stars and Geons
description: A ball of scalar field held together by its own gravity, the heir of John Wheeler's geon of light, found by David Kaup in 1968 and by Remo Ruffini and Silvano Bonazzola in 1969. The field turns in phase at a frequency $\omega$ while the spacetime stays static, with a regular centre and no horizon. The metric is known only numerically, as a solution of the Einstein-Klein-Gordon equations integrated outward from the centre, and the heaviest star has $M = 0.633\,M_P^2/m$ for bosons of mass $m$, with $M_P$ the Planck mass.
convention: We write the field of the star as $\varphi = \varphi_0(r)e^{i\omega t}$ for bosons of mass $m$, with $\mu = mc/\hbar$ and $\sigma = \sqrt{4\pi G}\,\varphi_0/c^2$ its dimensionless amplitude. We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\lambda{}_{\mu\lambda\nu}$.
history: Can light hold itself together? A burst of light has energy, and with the energy comes a mass that attracts [wheeler1955]. A bundle of it weighing between about $10^{39}$ and $10^{57}$ grams, John Archibald Wheeler reckoned in 1955, could be its own container, the pull of its mass "capable of holding the disturbance together for a time long in comparison with the characteristic periods of the system" [wheeler1955]. He named such "gravitational-electromagnetic entities" geons, and they gave him "a completely classical, divergence-free, self-consistent picture of the Newtonian concept of body" [wheeler1955]. A geon leaks, though, and Wheeler made the first estimates of the rate [wheeler1955]. A geon made of gravitational waves alone, Dieter Brill and James Hartle's of 1964, has "a finite lifetime" too [brillhartle1964, anderson1997].¶A lump of field that sits still does no better: for a wide class of nonlinear wave equations, G. H. Derrick showed in 1964, "there exist no stable time-independent solutions of finite energy" [derrick1964]. He wondered whether particles might be solutions "periodic in the time though the energy remains localized" [derrick1964]. David Kaup's ball of field of 1968 is one, held together by its own gravity: a complex scalar field with mass, $\varphi = \varphi_0(r)e^{i\omega t}$, turning like the hand of a clock at every point of space, all the hands in step [kaup1968, liebling2023]. The hands turn and the energy stays where it is, so the spacetime is static [liebling2023]. Kaup called his solutions Klein-Gordon geons [kaup1968]. David Feinblum and William McKinley's own, "similar to classical geons" and made of a Klein-Gordon field too, had reached the journal on 1 August 1967, seven months before Kaup's [feinblum1968, kaup1968].¶What holds a ball of field up against its own weight? Squeeze a boson of mass $m$ into a smaller space and its momentum grows, by the uncertainty principle, so the ball resists until it nears its own Schwarzschild radius, at a mass of about $0.5\,M_P^2/m$, where $M_P = \sqrt{\hbar c/G}$ is the Planck mass [liebling2023]. With $N$ bosons all in the ground state of a quantized field, Remo Ruffini and Silvano Bonazzola arrived in 1969 at Kaup's equations [ruffini1969, schunck2003]. The star has no equation of state: its stress along the radius differs from its stress across it, and "the usual concept of an equation of state breaks down" [ruffini1969, kaup1968]. Its metric is known only as numbers, found by shooting: choose the field at the centre and tune $\omega$ until an outward integration has the field die away far from the star [liebling2023, lai2004]. Ruffini and Bonazzola found a critical mass at about $(M_P/m)^2$ bosons, "above which mass gravitational collapse occurs", and numerically it comes to $0.633\,M_P^2/m$ [ruffini1969, liebling2023].¶For the bosons usually proposed that mass is far below the $M_P^3/m^2$ of a star of fermions, and Kaup's stars became "mini-boson stars" [liebling2023]. The name boson star dates from 1986, when Monica Colpi, Stuart Shapiro, and Ira Wasserman let the bosons repel one another through a potential $\tfrac{1}{4}\lambda|\varphi|^4$ and found masses "comparable to the Chandrasekhar mass for fermions", which "generally accepted astrophysical folklore" had ruled out [colpi1986, schunck2003]. Kaup had concluded that his geons "will not undergo spherically symmetric gravitational collapse", and offered them as "counterexamples to the conjecture that gravitational collapse is inevitable" [kaup1968]. Marcelo Gleiser and Richard Watkins took up the stability mode by mode and T. D. Lee and Yang Pang with a Hamiltonian, and in 1989 both pairs found the ground state stable up to the largest mass and unstable beyond it [gleiser1989, lee1989, liebling2023]. On Edward Seidel and Wai-Mo Suen's computer in 1990, disturbed stars past the largest mass either collapsed to a black hole or threw off field and settled among the stable ones [seidel1990, liebling2023].¶How would such a star form? The field equation has no viscous or dissipative term, so the only thing a collapsing cloud of field can shed is field [liebling2023]. The way out, which Seidel and Suen named gravitational cooling in 1994, is that the cloud throws part of itself off at each bounce and the remainder settles into a star [seidel1994, liebling2023]. A real field has no phase to turn and no static star, and its nearest relative is the oscillaton, in which the field and the spacetime both pulse [seidel1991, liebling2023]. A spinning boson star has an angular momentum that comes in whole multiples of its number of bosons, $J = kN$, and a field shaped like a ring [yoshida1997, liebling2023].¶Wheeler's geon was made of a field of spin one, and in 2016 Richard Brito, Vitor Cardoso, Carlos Herdeiro, and Eugen Radu gave such a field a mass and built Proca stars, "realizing Wheeler's concept of geons for an Abelian spin 1 field" [brito2016]. A boson star whose field does not couple to light gives off none, and in that respect "it resembles a BH, although it lacks a horizon", so it serves in models as a source of dark matter and as a black hole mimicker [liebling2023]. The gravitational wave signal GW190521, in the analysis of Juan Calderón Bustillo and eight collaborators, "is consistent with numerically simulated signals from head-on collisions of two (equal mass and spin) horizonless vector boson stars" [calderonbustillo2021]. Their fit puts the mass of the boson at $8.7 \times 10^{-13}$ eV [calderonbustillo2021]. Whether some of the stars already observed are boson stars is, for Steven Liebling and Carlos Palenzuela, "still an open question" [liebling2023].

related.text: The same balance for a star of fluid, where pressure does the holding up. Ruffini and Bonazzola put fermions through their method as well, and it "confirms the Oppenheimer-Volkoff treatment in extremely good approximation" [ruffini1969].

The star with no field in it: at $\sigma = 0$ the equations give $\alpha^2 = a^{-2} = 1 - r_s/r$. Far from a boson star the field has died away and the metric is Schwarzschild's for the star's mass [liebling2023].
The scalar field with no mass, at rest, which ends in a naked singularity at its centre [janis1968]. A boson star's field has a mass and a turning phase, and its centre is regular [liebling2023].
Mael Melvin's magnetic geon, parallel lines of magnetic field held together by their own gravity, Wheeler's idea in a cylinder [melvin1964].
A star held up by sideways stress alone, with none along its radius [einstein1939]. A boson star's two stresses differ as well, and neither star has an equation of state [ruffini1969].
Another star with no horizon offered as a stand in for a black hole, a ball of de Sitter space under a thin shell [mazur2004].

A ball of Yang-Mills field held together by its own gravity, also known only numerically. It comes as a ladder of solitons counted by the zeros of the field, and every one of them is unstable [bartnik1988, volkov1999].

Wheeler's geometrodynamics had a second way to get mass with no matter, the wormhole. Charles Misner's slice of 1960 has two masses at rest that are the two mouths of one wormhole in empty space [misner1957, misner1960].

Dieter Brill weighed a bundle of gravitational waves at one moment in 1959 and proved its mass positive [brill1959]. With James Hartle he built the gravitational geon five years later [brillhartle1964].

A spinning boson star can hold a small black hole at its centre, as long as the field turns with the horizon. Herdeiro and Radu's black holes run from Kerr's to spinning boson stars as the horizon shrinks to nothing [herdeiro2014].

coordinates.name: Polar Areal

parameters.description: Lapse, dimensionless: a clock held at radius $r$ runs at $\alpha$ of the rate $t$ counts. For the star it is known only numerically, as the solution of $\partial_r\alpha = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}\left[\dfrac{a^2 - 1}{r} + r\left(\left(\dfrac{\omega^2}{c^2\alpha^2} - \mu^2\right)a^2\sigma^2 + \left(\partial_r\sigma\right)^2\right)\right]$ that approaches $1$ far from the star

Radial function, dimensionless: $a\,dr$ is the proper distance along the radius, and $M(r) = c^2r\left(1 - a^{-2}\right)/2G$ is the mass inside the sphere of radius $r$. For the star it is known only numerically, as the solution of $\partial_r a = \dfrac{a}{2}\left[-\dfrac{a^2 - 1}{r} + r\left(\left(\dfrac{\omega^2}{c^2\alpha^2} + \mu^2\right)a^2\sigma^2 + \left(\partial_r\sigma\right)^2\right)\right]$ with $a(0) = 1$, where the field obeys $\partial_r^2\sigma = -\left(1 + a^2 - \mu^2r^2a^2\sigma^2\right)\dfrac{\partial_r\sigma}{r} - \left(\dfrac{\omega^2}{c^2\alpha^2} - \mu^2\right)a^2\sigma$

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ that Liebling and Palenzuela call polar areal, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. The lapse $\alpha(r)$ and the radial function $a(r)$ are dimensionless, and we leave both free. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Isotropic

parameters.description: Lapse, dimensionless, the same function of the sphere as in the polar areal chart: a clock held at radius $R$ runs at $\alpha$ of the rate $t$ counts, and $\alpha$ approaches $1$ far from the star

Conformal factor, dimensionless: the areal radius is $r = \psi^2R$, and the radial function of the polar areal chart is $a = \psi/\left(\psi + 2R\,\partial_R\psi\right)$. For the star it is known only numerically, from $dR/dr = aR/r$, and far from the star it approaches $1 + GM/(2c^2R)$, with $M$ the mass of the star

coordinates.convention: We use Liebling and Palenzuela's isotropic coordinates $(t, R, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $R$ the isotropic radius, a length, so the areal radius is $r = \psi^2R$. The lapse $\alpha(R)$ and the conformal factor $\psi(R)$ are dimensionless, and we leave both free. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
